rules.statement: Don't report the allocation and O(n) copy of an enumerator that snapshots a collection under its lock, or suggest a version-counter snapshot cache, when the member's remarks document that cost and no measured hot enumeration path exists.
rules.why: Snapshot enumeration under the lock is a deliberate thread-safety design, and a cache would add state and invalidation to every mutating member for a gain nobody has measured.
rules.check: Before reporting, read the GetEnumerator XML remarks for a documented copy cost and look for a benchmark or caller showing hot repeated enumeration; report only if the cost is undocumented or a measured hot path exists.

rules.statement: Don't flag the parameter count of generic state-passing factory overloads (for example T1 through T8) when they deliberately mirror an existing overload family of the same arities.
rules.why: Keeping parallel factories (such as sync and async variants) in step with matching arities is the intent, and a design decision may already record it.
rules.check: Before reporting a few-parameters violation on a generic overload, look for a sibling overload family with the same arities or an ADR that sets them; report only if the overload breaks that pattern or no such family exists.

rules.statement: Write XML doc summaries for integer state-flag fields in plain terms that state each value and when it holds, such as "Holds 1 after disposal has been requested and 0 before", instead of compressed wording like "One once …, zero before".
rules.why: Compressed wording in flag summaries is hard to parse and leaves readers unsure what the field's values mean.
rules.check: Look at <summary> comments on int fields used as flags (for example, ones set with Interlocked) for unclear phrasing that doesn't plainly give each value and the condition for it.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't ask for a named constant for a numeric wait-timeout literal that only serves as a safety cap ending a hung test.
rules.why: The named-constant rule covers repeated string literals, not numeric arguments, and a safety cap that no passing run reaches changes nothing a test asserts if its copies drift apart.
rules.check: Before reporting a bare TimeSpan or timeout literal in a test, check whether it's a string literal covered by the named-const rule or a timeout a test actually asserts on; don't report safety-cap timeouts passed to Wait or similar calls.
